text: Chapter 6, the key-value store. Let's see how it works in a few minutes.

A key-value store must answer two questions: which machine holds the data, and what happens when it fails. Partitioning uses consistent hashing to spread different keys across machines. That handles capacity. Replication stores each key on the next N machines clockwise, here N is three. That handles failure. With virtual nodes, replicas must land on different physical machines.

With three replicas, when is a write or a read successful? Look at three numbers. N is the number of replicas. W is how many acknowledgements a write waits for. R is how many replies a read waits for. Take N equals three, W and R both two. A write needs two acks, a read asks two replicas, and the two sets must share at least one node. So the reader sees the latest write. That is W plus R greater than N.

But overlapping does not mean you are safe. Say we write x equals one, and it reaches only replica A, short of the two acks. Read one asks A and B, and returns one. Right after, read two asks B and C, and sees only zero. Both reads satisfied R equals two, yet the user sees one, then zero. So the inequality is only part of the protocol. You also need version comparison and read repair.

Replicas can also be modified independently. The name starts as Zhang Min, with vector clock A one, B one. The network splits. A changes it to Zhang Ming, and its clock becomes A two, B one. Meanwhile B changes it to Li Min, and its clock becomes A one, B two. Whichever server changes the data adds one to its own entry.

How do we compare them? If every entry is no larger than the other's, it is an ancestor, and it is simply overwritten. If one side is larger in one entry and the other side in another, that is a concurrent conflict, called sibling versions. The vector clock only reports the conflict. It does not choose the winner. Say the user picks Zhang Ming. Take the maximum of each entry, then the executing server A adds one. The result is A three, B two.

Now, how a single storage node handles a write. Step one: append the write to the commit log, for crash recovery. Step two: put it into the in-memory table, the memtable. Step three: when memory reaches a threshold, flush it all to disk as a sorted SSTable. Once written, an SSTable is never modified.

A read goes the other way. Check memory first, and return on a hit. On a miss, we must search the SSTables on disk. But one key may be spread across several files, and reading them all is slow. So each SSTable gets a Bloom filter in front. It asks: could this key be in you? Any file that answers definitely not is skipped.

A Bloom filter is just a row of bits. Here, eight bits and two hash functions, for illustration. Insert alpha: set bits one and four. Insert beta: set bits four and six. Now query gamma, never inserted. It maps to bits one and six, both are one, so the filter can only say, maybe present. Another key maps to bits two and seven. Bit two is zero, so it is definitely absent.

Remember three things. N, W and R trade consistency against latency. Vector clocks detect conflicts, but do not decide who is right. And the commit log, memtable, SSTables and Bloom filters power reads and writes on a single node. Failure detection, hinted handoff and Merkle trees are in the book, and we only mention them here.
